Home News Arts and Culture Business Sports Opinion Research Live TV/Radio Media Elections Dark Mode Dark mode --> Child Online Africa calls for AU action on online violence against children Source : Myjoyonline.com 17 November 2026 11:20pm ▶ Listen to this article Audio By Carbonatix
Child Online Africa has called on the African Union (AU) and its member states to take urgent and coordinated action to protect children from online violence, sexual exploitation and other forms of digital abuse.
The organisation has launched the #AfricaESafetyNow campaign ahead of the Second Global Ministerial Conference on Ending Violence Against Children, scheduled for November 18 to 19, 2026, in Manila, Philippines.
In a statement issued on Tuesday, November 17, the organisation said Africa had reached a critical point in addressing the risks children face as they increasingly engage with digital platforms.
It acknowledged that technology provides opportunities for learning, innovation and development but warned that children are also exposed to online violence, cyberbullying, harmful content and sexual exploitation.
“The protection of children online can no longer be treated as an optional policy concern or left entirely to individual families. It is a shared responsibility that requires decisive leadership, coordinated continental action and accountability from governments and technology companies,” the statement said.
Child Online Africa wants the AU to move beyond policy commitments and establish concrete measures to protect children across digital spaces.
Its proposals include the development of a continental legal framework or protocol on child online safety, with clear and enforceable protection standards.
It is also calling for a dedicated African eSafety Commission, or an equivalent continental mechanism, to coordinate action and ensure accountability among member states.
The organisation further wants the AU to accelerate implementation of its Child Online Safety and Empowerment Policy through a clear and adequately funded roadmap.
Other recommendations include expanding age-appropriate digital literacy and online safety education in schools and communities, while strengthening the capacity of parents, teachers and caregivers.
It also urged governments to hold technology companies accountable through safety-by-design measures, stronger privacy safeguards, effective reporting systems and appropriate enforcement.
The organisation acknowledged the AU's adoption of its Child Online Safety and Empowerment Policy in 2024 as an important recognition of the need to protect children online.
However, it said the policy must now be backed by political commitment, institutional coordination and adequate investment.
“What is now required is the political will, institutional coordination, investment and accountability to translate that commitment into meaningful protection for children,” the statement said.
Ahead of the Manila conference, Child Online Africa said African countries should approach the discussions with a common position on protecting children from violence in both physical and digital environments.
It argued that online safety should form an integral part of the broader child protection agenda, rather than being treated as a separate concern.
“Violence against children does not end at the school gate or stop when a child enters the digital world. Online safety must be recognised as an integral part of the broader child protection agenda,” the statement said.
The organisation is calling on African governments, civil society groups, child-rights advocates, parents, educators, young people, development partners and technology companies to support the campaign.
It is urging the public to sign its petition, share its message and demand concrete action from the AU.
The petition, titled Africa's Children Are Under Attack Online: Demand the African Union Act Now to Save Them! , seeks to turn public concern into pressure for measurable policy action.
“Africa's children deserve more than promises. They deserve protection,” the statement said.
The statement was signed by Awo Aidam Amenyah, Executive Director of Child Online Africa, an Accra-based organisation advocating for child online protection across the continent.
